summary: Defines a new chunk type, several parameters, and procedures for SCTP so that chunks can be authenticated using shared keys between sender and receiver. The new parameters help establish those keys. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: SCTP is a transport protocol that carries many separate streams over one connection. This RFC adds a way for the two ends to prove that the control messages they exchange are genuine. Each side holds a shared key, and every message that needs protecting carries a code computed from that key, which the other side can check.

questions: how does the sctp auth chunk work
what is the sctp hmac-algo parameter
which hash algorithms does sctp auth support
how is the sctp association shared key computed
subtitle: Authenticating SCTP chunks with a shared key, so a sender can be sure the chunks came from its peer.

tldr.problem: SCTP's 32-bit verification tags protect an association against blind attackers, but they do not prove that a chunk really came from the peer, and TLS only protects SCTP user data.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds an AUTH chunk that carries an HMAC over itself and over every chunk that follows it in the packet, plus three parameters exchanged during setup so both ends can compute the same association shared key.
tldr.outcome: Without a pre-configured key the extension stops attackers who did not capture the handshake. With an endpoint pair shared key, even a man in the middle cannot inject chunks that require authentication.

today: RFC 4895 is a Proposed Standard on the Internet standards track, and no RFC in the site index obsoletes or updates it. It defines version 1 of the authentication extension, with SHA-1 as the algorithm every implementation must support and SHA-256 as the other defined option.

sections.title: Why SCTP Chunks Need Authenticating
sections.content:
SCTP uses 32-bit verification tags to protect itself against blind attackers. These values do not change during the lifetime of an SCTP association.

Looking at new SCTP extensions, there is a need for a method of proving that an SCTP chunk was really sent by the original peer that started the association, and not by a malicious attacker. Using Transport Layer Security, as defined in RFC 3436, does not help, because it only secures SCTP user data.

The extension presented in this document lets an SCTP sender authenticate chunks using shared keys between the sender and the receiver. The receiver can then verify that the chunks came from the sender and not from a malicious attacker, as long as the attacker does not know an association shared key.

The mechanism is an Hashed Message Authentication Code, or HMAC, which is a short code computed from a key and the data being protected. The RFC puts the result of the HMAC computation before the data it covers. Placing it at the end of the packet would have required placing a control chunk after DATA chunks when authenticating DATA chunks, which would break the rule that control chunks occur before DATA chunks in SCTP packets. Putting the result after the covered data would also stop the packet being sent while the HMAC was being computed, because the result is needed to compute the CRC32C checksum in the common header of the packet.

The SCTP extension for Dynamic Address Reconfiguration requires the use of this extension. The SCTP Partial Reliability extension can be used together with it.
sections.plainLanguage: The tags that SCTP already uses stop strangers from guessing their way into a connection, but they do not prove who sent a particular message. TLS does not help either, because it only covers the data the application sends. This RFC adds a short code, computed from a shared key, that is placed in front of the messages it protects.

sections.title: The Three New Parameters
sections.content:
Three new parameter types are used to negotiate the authentication during association setup. The parameter format requires the receiver to ignore a parameter it does not understand and carry on processing, which is achieved by the use of the upper bits of the parameter type.

The Random Parameter (RANDOM), type 0x8002, carries a random number of arbitrary length. Its parameter length is the length of the random number plus 4. If the random number is not a multiple of 4 bytes, the sender MUST pad the parameter with zero bytes to make it 32-bit aligned, and the padding, at most 3 bytes long, MUST be ignored by the receiver. The RANDOM parameter MUST be included once in the INIT or INIT-ACK chunk, if the sender wants to send or receive authenticated chunks, to provide a 32-byte random number. For a 32-byte random number the padding is empty.

The Chunk List Parameter (CHUNKS), type 0x8003, specifies which chunk types are required to be authenticated before being sent by the peer. Each listed chunk type is one byte, and the parameter length is the number of listed chunk types plus 4. The parameter MUST be included once in the INIT or INIT-ACK chunk if the sender wants to receive authenticated chunks, and its maximum length is 260 bytes. The chunk types for INIT, INIT-ACK, SHUTDOWN-COMPLETE and AUTH MUST NOT be listed in it; if a CHUNKS parameter is received, those types MUST be ignored.

The Requested HMAC Algorithm Parameter (HMAC-ALGO), type 0x8004, lists the HMAC identifiers the peer MUST use. Each identifier is two bytes, and the parameter length is the number of identifiers multiplied by 2, plus 4. The values are listed by preference, with the first one the most preferable to the sender. The parameter MUST be included once in the INIT or INIT-ACK chunk if the sender wants to send or receive authenticated chunks.
sections.plainLanguage: Three parameters are added to the setup exchange. One carries a random number, one lists the message types that must be authenticated, and one lists the hashing algorithms the sender is willing to accept, best first.

sections.title: HMAC Identifiers and the Error Cause
sections.content:
Four HMAC identifiers are defined at present. The value 0 is reserved, 1 is SHA-1, 2 is reserved and 3 is SHA-256. Every endpoint supporting SCTP chunk authentication MUST support the HMAC based on the SHA-1 algorithm.

If an AUTH chunk is received with an HMAC identifier the endpoint does not support, the endpoint reports it with a new error cause, the Unsupported HMAC Identifier error cause, whose cause code is 0x0105 and whose cause length is 6. It carries the two-byte HMAC identifier that was not supported, followed by two bytes of padding, which the sender MUST fill with zero bytes and which the receiver MUST ignore.
sections.plainLanguage: Only a few hashing algorithms are named, and SHA-1 is the one every implementation must have. If a peer uses one the receiver does not know, the receiver reports it with a dedicated error message and drops the packet.

sections.title: The Authentication Chunk
sections.content:
The new chunk type is the Authentication Chunk, AUTH, with the value 0x0F. The format requires the receiver to ignore the chunk if it is not understood and silently discard all the chunks that follow it, which is achieved by the use of the upper bits of the chunk type.

The chunk holds the result of the HMAC calculation. Its type field is one byte and MUST be set to 0x0F. The flags field is one byte, SHOULD be set to zero on transmit and MUST be ignored on receipt. The length field is two bytes and holds the length of the HMAC in bytes plus 8. The Shared Key Identifier is two bytes and describes which endpoint pair shared key is used. The HMAC Identifier is two bytes and describes which message digest is being used. The HMAC itself is n bytes, and if its length is not a multiple of 4 bytes the sender MUST pad the chunk with zero bytes to make it 32-bit aligned, with padding of at most 3 bytes that the receiver MUST ignore.

The AUTH control chunk MUST NOT appear more than once in an SCTP packet. All control and data chunks placed after the AUTH chunk in the packet are sent in an authenticated way, while chunks placed before it are not authenticated. DATA chunks cannot appear before control chunks in an SCTP packet.
sections.plainLanguage: The AUTH chunk goes at the front of the protected part of the packet. It names the key and the algorithm used, and carries the resulting code. Everything after it in the same packet is covered by that code.

sections.title: Establishing the Association Shared Key
sections.content:
An SCTP endpoint willing to receive or send authenticated chunks MUST send one RANDOM parameter in its INIT or INIT-ACK chunk, and the RANDOM parameter MUST contain a 32-byte random number. If the random number is not 32 bytes, the association MUST be aborted, and the ABORT chunk SHOULD contain the error cause 'Protocol Violation'. In case of an INIT collision, the rules for handling this random number follow the same pattern as those for the Verification Tag, so each endpoint knows its own random number and the peer's after the association is established.

Each endpoint keeps a list of chunk types it only accepts if they arrive in an authenticated way. The list is included in the INIT and INIT-ACK and MAY be omitted if it is empty. Because the list does not change during the lifetime of the endpoint, there is no problem in case of an INIT collision. Each endpoint MUST also include a HMAC-ALGO parameter listing the HMAC identifiers it requests the peer to use. The receiver of an HMAC-ALGO parameter SHOULD use the first listed algorithm it supports, the HMAC algorithm based on SHA-1 MUST be supported and included, and an endpoint MUST NOT change the parameters it listed during its lifetime.

Both endpoints MAY have endpoint pair shared keys, which are byte vectors that are pre-configured or established by another mechanism and are identified by the Shared Key Identifier. For each endpoint pair shared key, an association shared key is computed. If there is no endpoint pair shared key, only one association shared key is computed, using an empty byte vector as the endpoint pair shared key.

The RANDOM, CHUNKS and HMAC-ALGO parameters sent by each endpoint are concatenated as byte vectors, including the parameter type, the parameter length and the parameter value but with all padding removed. Parameters that were not sent are simply omitted. The two resulting vectors are the two key vectors.

The association shared key is then computed from the endpoint pair shared keys and the key vectors: the numerically smaller key vector is concatenated to the endpoint pair shared key, and the numerically larger key vector is concatenated to that. If the key vectors are equal as numbers but differ in length, the order is the endpoint shared key, then the shorter key vector, then the longer one. Otherwise the key vectors are identical and may be concatenated to the endpoint pair key in any order. All numerical comparisons use network byte order.
sections.plainLanguage: Both ends combine the three parameters they exchanged, sort them into a fixed order, and mix that with a shared key to get the key they will use for this connection. Doing it in a fixed order means both ends compute the same key even though each of them sent its own parameters.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving Authenticated Chunks
sections.content:
Endpoints MUST send all requested chunks that have been authenticated where the peer has requested this. The other chunks MAY be sent whether or not they have been authenticated. If endpoint pair shared keys are used, one of them MUST be selected for authentication.

To send chunks in an authenticated way, the sender MUST include them after an AUTH chunk, which means that a sender MUST bundle chunks in order to authenticate them. If the endpoint has no endpoint pair shared key for the peer, it MUST use Shared Key Identifier zero with an empty endpoint pair shared key. With multiple endpoint shared keys, the sender selects one and uses the corresponding identifier.

The sender computes the Message Authentication Code as described in RFC 2104, using the hash function named by the HMAC Identifier and the shared association key. The data used for the computation is the AUTH chunk with its HMAC field set to zero, followed by all the chunks that are placed after the AUTH chunk in the SCTP packet. All fields are in network byte order, and the padding of all the chunks being authenticated MUST be included in the computation. The sender then fills the HMAC into the HMAC field and sends the packet.

The receiver has a list of chunk types that it expects to receive only after an AUTH chunk, which it sent to the peer during association setup, and it MUST silently discard those chunks if they are not placed after an AUTH chunk. It MUST use the HMAC algorithm indicated in the HMAC Identifier field. If that algorithm was not specified by the receiver in its HMAC-ALGO parameter during setup, the AUTH chunk and all the chunks after it MUST be discarded and an ERROR chunk SHOULD be sent with the Unsupported HMAC Identifier error cause.

If an endpoint with no shared key receives a Shared Key Identifier other than 0, it MUST silently discard all authenticated chunks. If it has at least one endpoint pair shared key for the peer, it MUST use the key specified by the Shared Key Identifier if one has been configured for it, and if none has been configured, all authenticated chunks MUST be silently discarded. The receiver then performs the same calculation as the sender. If the result matches the HMAC field, all the chunks following the AUTH chunk are processed; if it does not match, they MUST all be silently discarded. If the receiver wants to tear down an association in an authenticated way only, handling of malformed packets should not result in tearing the association down.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender computes a code over the AUTH chunk itself and over every chunk that follows it, then sends the packet. The receiver repeats the calculation and compares the results. A mismatch means the chunks are thrown away without a reply, so an attacker learns nothing from the failure.

sections.title: Example Exchanges
sections.content:
The simplest way of using the extension is the following exchange, where the parameters in brackets are the ones this RFC adds.

---------- INIT[RANDOM; CHUNKS; HMAC-ALGO] ---------->
<------- INIT-ACK[RANDOM; CHUNKS; HMAC-ALGO] ---------
-------------------- COOKIE-ECHO -------------------->
<-------------------- COOKIE-ACK ---------------------

The CHUNKS parameter is optional in the INIT and INIT-ACK. If the server wants to receive DATA chunks in an authenticated way, the exchange can be:

---------- INIT[RANDOM; CHUNKS; HMAC-ALGO] ---------->
<------- INIT-ACK[RANDOM; CHUNKS; HMAC-ALGO] ---------
--------------- COOKIE-ECHO; AUTH; DATA ------------->
<----------------- COOKIE-ACK; SACK ------------------

The RFC notes that if the endpoint pair shared key depends on the client and the server and is only known by the upper layer, this exchange requires upper layer intervention between the processing of the COOKIE-ECHO chunk and the processing of the AUTH and DATA chunk at the server side. That intervention may be realised by a COMMUNICATION-UP notification followed by the presentation of the endpoint pair shared key by the upper layer to the SCTP stack. If the intervention is not possible because of limitations of the API, for example the socket API, the server might discard the AUTH and DATA chunk, making a retransmission of the DATA chunk necessary. If the same endpoint pair shared key is used for multiple endpoints and does not depend on the client, the intervention might not be necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: In the simplest case the extra parameters ride along in the normal setup exchange and nothing else changes. To protect the data itself, the server sends its cookie back together with an AUTH chunk and the first data chunk in one packet.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Without endpoint shared keys, this extension only protects against modification or injection of authenticated chunks by attackers who did not capture the initial handshake that set up the SCTP association.

If an endpoint pair shared key is used, even a true man in the middle cannot inject chunks that are required to be authenticated, even if he intercepts the initial message exchange. The endpoint also then knows that it is accepting authenticated chunks from a peer who knows the endpoint pair shared key. The establishment of endpoint pair shared keys is out of the scope of this document; other mechanisms can be used, such as TLS or manual configuration.

When an endpoint accepts COOKIE-ECHO chunks only in an authenticated way, the restart procedure does not work: neither an attacker nor a restarted endpoint that does not know the association shared key can perform a restart. If the association shared key is known, a restart is possible. The RFC also notes in the procedures that requiring ABORT chunks and COOKIE-ECHO chunks to be authenticated makes it impossible for an attacker to bring down or restart an association, but that an endpoint accepting ABORT chunks only in an authenticated way may take longer to detect that the peer is no longer available.

Three further points close the section. Because SCTP already has a built-in mechanism that handles the reception of duplicated chunks, the solution makes use of that and does not provide a way to avoid replay attacks by itself; a separate shared key is used for each association so that replay attacks cannot cover more than one association. Each endpoint presenting a list of more than one element in its HMAC-ALGO parameter must be prepared for the peer choosing the weakest algorithm listed. And when an endpoint pair uses non-NULL endpoint pair shared keys but one of the endpoints still accepts a NULL key, an attacker who captured the initial handshake can still inject or modify authenticated chunks by using the NULL key.
sections.plainLanguage: The protection depends on the key. Without a pre-configured key, an attacker who watched the setup can still forge messages. With one, even an attacker sitting in the middle cannot. Requiring authenticated cookie echoes also blocks restarts, which is a trade-off. Replayed old messages are handled by SCTP itself, and a peer may pick the weakest algorithm you offered.

messages.note: The AUTH chunk covers itself and the DATA chunk that follows it.

viz.caption: WHAT EACH ENDPOINT MUST DO AT SETUP

items.title: Send a RANDOM parameter
items.text: One in the INIT or INIT-ACK, carrying a 32-byte random number.

items.title: Send an HMAC-ALGO parameter
items.text: Listing the acceptable algorithms, best first. SHA-1 must be included.

items.title: Offer a CHUNKS parameter
items.text: Listing the chunk types the peer must authenticate before sending.

items.title: Keep the list fixed
items.text: An endpoint must not change what it listed in HMAC-ALGO during its lifetime.
